mcq.q: A new law on "contracts and partnership" is needed. Under the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, who can make it?
options: Only Parliament, as it is in the Union List
Only State Legislatures, as it is in the State List
Both Parliament and State Legislatures, as the subject is in the Concurrent List
mcq.explain: Contracts, including partnership and agency, is an entry in the Concurrent List (List III). Both Parliament and the State Legislatures may legislate on it; if a State law conflicts with a Central law on a Concurrent subject, the Central law generally prevails. That is why the Contract Act and Partnership Act are Central Acts that States may amend.
mcq.topic: Division of law-making power: three lists
mcq.fast: Commercial laws like contracts, partnership and insolvency = Concurrent List. Courts never "make" statutes — strike that option first.

mcq.q: Power to make laws on a subject that is NOT mentioned in any of the three lists (residuary power) belongs to:
mcq.explain: Residuary power — the power to legislate on matters not listed in the Union, State or Concurrent Lists — is given to Parliament by Article 248 read with the Union List. This keeps new subjects, such as many technology-related matters, with the Centre and reflects the strong-Centre design of Indian federalism.
mcq.topic: Division of law-making power: three lists
mcq.fast: Residuary = Parliament (Art. 248). The President and courts do not legislate.

mcq.q: Which subject is in the State List?
mcq.explain: Police and public order are State List subjects, so each State runs its own police force. Defence and banking are Union List subjects, and criminal law is in the Concurrent List, where both levels can legislate. Remember the logic: matters of local administration go to States; national security and money go to the Union.
mcq.topic: Division of law-making power: three lists
mcq.fast: Local administration (police, public order, agriculture, public health) = State. Defence/banking = Union. Criminal law = Concurrent.

mcq.q: A Money Bill can be introduced:
options: Only in a joint sitting of both Houses
mcq.explain: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only on the recommendation of the President. The Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend it; it may only make recommendations within 14 days, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha decides whether a bill is a Money Bill.
mcq.topic: How a law is made
mcq.fast: Money = people's House = Lok Sabha only. There is no joint sitting for a Money Bill.

mcq.q: A bill passed by both Houses of Parliament becomes an Act when:
options: It is published in a newspaper
The President gives assent to it
mcq.explain: After a bill is passed by both Houses, it is sent to the President. Only when the President gives assent (Article 111) does the bill become an Act. The courts have no role in approving bills; they may later examine whether an Act is constitutional if someone challenges it.
mcq.topic: How a law is made
mcq.fast: Last step of law-making = President's assent. Courts review laws afterwards, they never approve bills.

mcq.q: When Parliament is not in session and immediate action is needed, the President can make law by issuing:
options: A gazette circular of the RBI
mcq.explain: Under Article 123 the President may promulgate an ordinance when both Houses are not in session and immediate action is necessary. An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament, but it must be laid before Parliament when it reassembles and lapses six weeks after reassembly unless approved.
mcq.topic: How a law is made
mcq.fast: Law by the executive while Parliament is away = ordinance (Art. 123). Writs are court orders.

mcq.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes criminal law from civil law?
options: Criminal cases always end in compensation, civil cases in jail terms
In a criminal case the State prosecutes the accused, while in a civil case the aggrieved person brings the suit
Civil cases must be proved beyond reasonable doubt
Only civil wrongs are offences against society
mcq.explain: A crime is treated as a wrong against society, so the State prosecutes and the punishment is imprisonment or fine, proved beyond reasonable doubt. A civil wrong is a private dispute; the injured person files the suit and seeks remedies like damages or injunction, decided on the balance of probabilities.
mcq.topic: Types of law: criminal and civil
mcq.fast: Criminal = State v. accused, punishment. Civil = person v. person, compensation. Any option that swaps these is wrong.

mcq.q: In a judgment, the part that is binding on lower courts as precedent is the:
mcq.explain: The ratio decidendi is the legal principle on which the decision is based, and it binds lower courts under the doctrine of stare decisis. Obiter dicta are remarks made "by the way"; they are only persuasive. A dissenting opinion is not the decision of the court at all, so it binds no one.
mcq.topic: Common law, precedent and stare decisis
mcq.fast: Ratio = reason = rule (binding). Obiter = "by the way" (persuasive only).

mcq.q: Assertion (A): The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India.  Reason (R): Article 141 of the Constitution gives the Supreme Court's decisions binding force.
options: A and R are both true; R does not explain A
A is true; R is false
A and R are both true; R explains A
A is false; R is true
mcq.explain: Both statements are true, and R directly explains A. Article 141 states that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India. This is the constitutional basis of the doctrine of precedent at the top of the Indian judicial system.
mcq.topic: Common law, precedent and stare decisis
mcq.fast: If R names the very Article that creates A, the answer is "both true, R explains A".

mcq.q: The principle "audi alteram partem" means:
options: No one should be condemned unheard — hear the other side
No one should be a judge in his own cause
Ignorance of law is no excuse
mcq.explain: Audi alteram partem means "hear the other side": before an adverse decision, the affected person must get notice and a fair chance to present his case. The rule against bias is a different principle of natural justice, expressed as nemo judex in causa sua — no one should be a judge in his own cause.
mcq.topic: Principles of natural justice
mcq.fast: Audi = hear (think "audio"). Nemo judex = no bias.

mcq.q: A disciplinary committee includes the very officer whose complaint started the inquiry. Which principle of natural justice is violated?
options: Rule against bias (nemo judex in causa sua)
mcq.explain: A person who is a party to the dispute, or who has an interest in its outcome, should not decide it. When the complainant sits on the committee, the rule against bias — nemo judex in causa sua — is broken, even if the accused was given a hearing. Stare decisis and caveat emptor are not natural-justice principles.
mcq.topic: Principles of natural justice
mcq.fast: Interested person deciding = bias. A missing hearing would be audi alteram partem.

mcq.q: A custom is accepted by courts as a source of law only if it is:
options: Ancient, certain, reasonable and not against law or morality
Followed by at least one generation of a family
Approved in advance by the Supreme Court
mcq.explain: Custom is one of the oldest sources of Indian law, but courts enforce a custom only when it has been followed for a very long time, is clear and certain, is reasonable, and does not conflict with statute law, public policy or morality. A custom that fails any of these tests is not applied.
mcq.topic: Sources of law in India
mcq.fast: Custom test = old + certain + reasonable + lawful. Courts do not "pre-approve" customs.

mcq.q: Rules framed by a Ministry under powers given to it by a parent Act are called:
mcq.explain: Parliament often lays down policy in an Act and lets the executive fill in details through rules, regulations and notifications. Such law made by a delegate under the parent Act is delegated or subordinate legislation, for example rules under the Companies Act, 2013 made by the Central Government.
mcq.topic: Sources of law in India
mcq.fast: Made by the executive under an Act = delegated. Ordinance is made without a parent Act when Parliament is not sitting.

mcq.q: A citizen whose fundamental right is violated may move the Supreme Court directly by a writ petition under:
mcq.explain: Article 32 gives every person the right to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of fundamental rights, and it is itself a fundamental right. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs, for fundamental rights and also for other purposes. Article 141 deals with precedent and Article 123 with ordinances.
mcq.topic: Structure of the Indian judicial system
mcq.fast: Supreme Court writs = 32; High Court writs = 226 (wider scope).

mcq.q: Which writ is issued to produce before the court a person who is detained, so that the legality of the detention can be examined?
mcq.explain: Habeas corpus literally means "have the body"; the court orders the detaining authority to produce the person and justify the detention. Mandamus commands a public authority to perform a duty, quo warranto questions a person's right to hold a public office, and certiorari quashes the order of a lower court or tribunal.
mcq.topic: Structure of the Indian judicial system
mcq.fast: Detained person = "body" = habeas corpus. Mandamus = "we command" a duty.

mcq.q: Match the writ with its purpose. (i) Mandamus (ii) Quo warranto (iii) Prohibition (iv) Certiorari — (a) stops a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction in a pending case (b) quashes a decision already made by a lower court without jurisdiction (c) orders a public official to perform a public duty (d) asks "by what authority" a person holds a public office
mcq.explain: Mandamus commands performance of a public duty; quo warranto asks by what authority someone holds a public office; prohibition is issued while a case is still pending to stop a lower court from going beyond its jurisdiction; certiorari quashes an order already passed without jurisdiction. Prohibition prevents, certiorari cures.
mcq.topic: Structure of the Indian judicial system
mcq.fast: Fix the two sure ones (mandamus-duty, quo warranto-office), then: prohibition = before decision, certiorari = after.

mcq.q: The highest court in a district for civil matters is generally the:
options: Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate
mcq.explain: In each district the court of the District Judge is the principal civil court of original jurisdiction; on the criminal side the Sessions Court heads the district. The Chief Judicial Magistrate is a criminal court below the Sessions Court, a Lok Adalat is a settlement forum, and the High Court is the State-level court above the district.
mcq.topic: Structure of the Indian judicial system
mcq.fast: District level civil head = District Judge; criminal head = Sessions Judge. High Court is State level, not district level.

mcq.q: The maximum number of judges of the Supreme Court of India, including the Chief Justice, as presently fixed by law is:
mcq.explain: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, as amended in 2019, fixes the strength at 33 judges plus the Chief Justice of India — 34 in all. The Constitution originally provided for a Chief Justice and seven other judges, and Parliament has increased the number several times as the workload grew.
mcq.topic: Structure of the Indian judicial system
mcq.fast: Remember "33 + CJI = 34" (2019 increase).

mcq.q: The regulator of the securities market in India, set up to protect investors and develop and regulate the market, is:
mcq.explain: SEBI, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, got statutory status by the SEBI Act, 1992. Its mandate is to protect the interests of investors in securities and to promote the development of, and regulate, the securities market. The RBI regulates banks and money, IBBI the insolvency process, and IRDAI insurance.
mcq.topic: Major regulators: SEBI, RBI and IBBI
mcq.fast: Securities = SEBI; banks/currency = RBI; insolvency = IBBI; insurance = IRDAI.

mcq.q: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) was established under:
options: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
mcq.explain: IBBI was set up under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. It regulates insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies and information utilities, and frames regulations for insolvency resolution and liquidation processes. Its name itself points to the Code under which it was created.
mcq.topic: Major regulators: SEBI, RBI and IBBI
mcq.fast: The Board takes the name of its statute: Insolvency Board -> Insolvency Code, 2016.

mcq.q: Pick the task that the RBI does NOT perform:
options: Acting as banker to the Government
Registering companies and approving their memorandum
mcq.explain: The RBI formulates monetary policy, issues currency notes, acts as banker to the Central and State Governments, and regulates banks and NBFCs. Registration of companies is done by the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 2013, administered by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs — not by the RBI.
mcq.topic: Major regulators: SEBI, RBI and IBBI
mcq.fast: Company registration = ROC/MCA. Everything about money, banks and government accounts = RBI.

mcq.q: The Companies Act, 2013 and the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 are administered by the:
mcq.explain: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) administers the Companies Act, 2013, the LLP Act, 2008 and related laws, mainly through the Registrars of Companies, the Regional Directors and other offices. Students should link corporate and LLP registration with the MCA, and banking regulation with the RBI.
mcq.topic: Enforcing the law: the executive and key ministries
mcq.fast: Company or LLP = "Corporate Affairs".

mcq.q: An appeal against an order of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) lies to the:
mcq.explain: Under the Companies Act, 2013, a person aggrieved by an order of the NCLT may appeal to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), and an appeal from the NCLAT lies to the Supreme Court on a question of law. The District Court and Registrar have no appellate role over the Tribunal.
mcq.topic: Structure of the Indian judicial system
mcq.fast: Tribunal -> Appellate Tribunal -> Supreme Court.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): A criminal case is filed in the name of the State.  Reason (R): Crimes are regarded as wrongs against society as a whole.
options: A and R are both true; R explains A
A and R are both true; R does not explain A
A is true; R is false
A is false; R is true
mcq.explain: Both are true and R explains A. Because a crime is regarded as a wrong against society, not merely against the victim, the State takes up the prosecution — which is why criminal cases are titled "State v. accused". In a civil case the injured individual sues in his own name.
mcq.topic: Types of law: criminal and civil
mcq.fast: Ask "does R give the reason WHY A happens?" Here yes — society is wronged, so the State prosecutes.

mcq.q: Under the doctrine of stare decisis, a High Court is bound by:
options: The decisions of all other High Courts
The decisions of the Supreme Court
The decisions of district courts in its State
mcq.explain: Stare decisis means "stand by what has been decided". A court is bound by the decisions of courts above it in the hierarchy. A High Court must follow the Supreme Court. Decisions of other High Courts and of foreign courts are only persuasive, and decisions of lower courts never bind a higher court.
mcq.topic: Common law, precedent and stare decisis
mcq.fast: Precedent binds downward only. Other High Courts and foreign courts = persuasive.

mcq.q: Which subject belongs to the Union List?
mcq.explain: Foreign affairs, defence, atomic energy, railways, banking and currency are Union List subjects on which only Parliament can legislate. Public health and sanitation, agriculture and police are State List subjects, because they are best handled close to the people by each State government.
mcq.topic: Division of law-making power: three lists
mcq.fast: National, outward-facing matters = Union. Local, everyday administration = State.

mcq.q: Judges of the Supreme Court of India are appointed by:
options: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
mcq.explain: Article 124(2) of the Constitution provides that every judge of the Supreme Court is appointed by the President. In practice the President acts on the recommendation of the collegium of senior judges of the Supreme Court. The Prime Minister, the Speaker and the Law Minister do not make the appointment themselves.
mcq.topic: Structure of the Indian judicial system
mcq.fast: Constitutional appointments of judges are made in the President's name.
